hypotheses.title: FxERC20RootTunnel.syncWithdraw allows anyone to drain all bridged tokens
hypotheses.description: `syncWithdraw` has no access control and no verification that the caller is the authorized child tunnel / fxManager. Any external account can call it with an arbitrary `rootToken` and `amount`, and the contract will transfer tokens held by the tunnel to the caller. Since `deposit` accumulates user funds in this contract, the entire balance is at risk.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Users deposit tokens via `deposit(rootToken, amount)`. 2) Attacker calls `syncWithdraw(rootToken, IERC20(rootToken).balanceOf(address(this)))`. 3) Contract transfers the full balance to the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of all bridged/deposited tokens held by the tunnel.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `syncWithdraw` to the trusted fxManager/child tunnel (e.g., `onlyFxManager`) and validate the message origin.

hypotheses.title: FxERC20ChildTunnel.syncDeposit mints unlimited tokens to any caller
hypotheses.description: `syncDeposit` has no access control and no verification that the caller is the authorized root tunnel / fxManager. Any external account can call it with an arbitrary `childToken` and `amount`, causing `BMWTokenChild.mint(msg.sender, amount)` to be invoked. The child token's `mint` only checks `msg.sender == _fxManager`, and the tunnel is the fxManager, so the tunnel's lack of access control is the entire barrier.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `syncDeposit(childToken, hugeAmount)`. 2) Tunnel calls `childToken.mint(attacker, hugeAmount)`. 3) Attacker receives arbitrary minted tokens and can dump them.
hypotheses.impact: Unlimited inflation of the bridged token, draining value from all holders and any liquidity pools.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `syncDeposit` to the trusted fxManager/root tunnel and validate the message origin.

hypotheses.title: AgentToken.initialize callable by anyone to seize ownership of clone
hypotheses.description: `initialize` is `external initializer` with no access control. The factory clones the implementation and immediately calls `initialize`, but between the `Clones.clone` and the `initialize` call the clone is uninitialized and any external actor can front-run the factory's `initialize` call. The attacker supplies their own `integrationAddresses_`/`baseParams_` and becomes `owner()` via `_transferOwnership(projectOwner_)`, and also sets `_factory = _msgSender()` (the attacker), giving them full control of the token (tax rates, tax recipient, valid callers, liquidity pools, withdraw functions).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes factory `_createNewAgentToken` (or `AgentMigrator._createNewAgentToken`) about to clone+initialize. 2) Attacker front-runs the factory's `initialize` transaction on the freshly deployed clone with their own params. 3) `initializer` succeeds, attacker becomes owner and `_factory`. 4) Factory's subsequent `initialize` reverts, but the token is already attacker-controlled; attacker can set tax recipient to themselves, add arbitrary valid callers, drain via `withdrawERC20`/`withdrawETH`, and manipulate `addInitialLiquidity`.
hypotheses.impact: Complete takeover of newly created AgentToken: theft of tax tokens, LP tokens, and any ERC20/ETH held by the token; broken agent creation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `initialize` to the factory (e.g., `require(_msgSender() == expectedFactory)` set in constructor or use an `onlyFactory` modifier), or have the factory deploy and initialize atomically via `Clones.cloneDeterministic` + `initialize` in the same tx with a factory-only guard.

hypotheses.title: AgentVeToken.initialize callable by anyone on fresh clone
hypotheses.description: `initialize` is `external initializer` with no caller restriction. The factory clones `veTokenImplementation` and calls `initialize` in a separate transaction step; an attacker can front-run and initialize the clone with themselves as `founder`, `assetToken`, `agentNft`, and `canStake`. Once initialized, the attacker controls `setCanStake`, `setMatureAt` (via ADMIN_ROLE on the fake `agentNft`), and the founder-only withdrawal path.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker watches mempool for factory `_createNewAgentVeToken`. 2) Front-runs with `initialize(name, symbol, attacker, attackerToken, 0, attackerNft, true)`. 3) Attacker becomes `founder`; factory's `initialize` reverts. 4) Attacker can call `setCanStake`, and if they control `agentNft` (their own contract) they can grant themselves ADMIN_ROLE to call `setMatureAt`, and drain staked `assetToken` via `withdraw` once `matureAt` is set to 0.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of staked LP/asset tokens from the veToken contract; broken agent staking/DAO setup.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a factory-only guard to `initialize` (e.g., store expected factory in constructor and `require(_msgSender() == factory)`), or deploy+initialize atomically.

hypotheses.title: AgentTax dcaSell minOutput computed on taxToken amount not asset output
hypotheses.description: In `dcaSell`, `minOutput = ((amountToSwap * (DENOM - slippage)) / DENOM)` is computed on `amountToSwap`, which is denominated in `taxToken`, but `minOutput` is passed to `_swapForAsset` as the minimum output of `assetToken`. Since `taxToken` and `assetToken` are different tokens with different prices, `minOutput` is dimensionally wrong. If `taxToken` is worth much less than `assetToken`, `minOutput` will be far below the fair output, allowing the swap to execute at a terrible rate (or revert if the router enforces it). Conversely, if `taxToken` is worth more, `minOutput` may exceed the fair output and cause the swap to revert, blocking tax collection.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or MEV bot) observes a pending `dcaSell` call. 2) Attacker sandwiches the swap in the AMM to push the price against the contract. 3) Because `minOutput` is computed on the wrong token amount, the slippage check is ineffective, and the contract sells tax tokens at a manipulated low price. 4) Attacker profits from the price impact.
hypotheses.impact: Tax tokens sold at manipulated prices; creator/treasury receive less asset token; value extracted by MEV.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `minOutput` from `router.getAmountsOut(amountToSwap, path)[1]` and apply slippage to that value.

hypotheses.title: AgentToken tax auto-swap uses amountOutMin=0, enabling sandwich drain
hypotheses.description: `_swapTax` calls `swapExactTokensForTokensSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens(swapBalance_, 0, path, ...)` with an `amountOutMin_` of 0. There is no on-chain price check, oracle, or minimum-out enforcement anywhere else in the token. Every taxable transfer that crosses `swapThresholdInTokens` (or any caller who pushes `balanceOf(address(this))` above the threshold) triggers a router swap that will accept any output, including near-zero.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes mempool for any AgentToken transfer where `_eligibleForSwap` will be true. 2) Attacker front-runs by swapping large pairToken into the pool to push the AgentToken price down. 3) Victim transaction executes, router sells accumulated tax tokens for a tiny amount of pairToken (0 min out), funds routed to `projectTaxRecipient`. 4) Attacker back-runs, restoring the pool price and pocketing the difference.
hypotheses.impact: Systematic loss of the tax pool that is meant for the project/creator. Attack can be repeated on every eligible transfer, materially draining value intended for the tax recipient.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pass a non-zero `amountOutMin` derived from a trusted TWAP/oracle, or accept a caller-supplied min-out that is validated against a reference price.

hypotheses.title: Genesis.onGenesisFailed can be permanently bricked by a single participant
hypotheses.description: The function iterates over `participantIndexes` and refunds each participant, incrementing `refundUserCountForFailed` only when `mapAddrToVirtuals[participant] > 0`. The final `isFailed = true` is only set when `refundUserCountForFailed == participants.length`. If any participant's `mapAddrToVirtuals` was already zeroed (e.g., via a prior partial call, or if a participant address appears twice in the array), the counter will never reach `participants.length`, so `isFailed` can never be set and the genesis can never be finalized as failed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker participates with a tiny amount. 2) Attacker calls `onGenesisFailed` with an array that includes their own index twice (or includes an index whose `mapAddrToVirtuals` is already 0). 3) The first pass zeroes their balance and increments the counter; the second pass sees `virtualsAmt == 0` and skips incrementing. 4) `refundUserCountForFailed` is now permanently less than `participants.length`, so `isFailed` can never become true. 5) All other participants' funds remain locked in the Genesis contract forever because `withdrawLeftAssetsAfterFinalized` requires `whenFinalized` (which requires `isFailed || isCancelled || agentTokenAddress != address(0)`).
hypotheses.impact: All contributed virtual tokens are permanently stuck in the Genesis contract; no refunds possible, no finalization possible.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track refunded participants via a mapping/bitmap instead of a counter, or set `isFailed = true` when all entries in `participants` have zero balances rather than relying on a counter that can be desynced.

hypotheses.title: FxERC20ChildTunnel.withdraw burns tokens from arbitrary user without allowance
hypotheses.description: `withdraw` has no access control and no allowance check. Any external account can call `withdraw(childToken, amount)` and the tunnel will invoke `BMWTokenChild.burn(msg.sender, amount)`. Because the tunnel is the fxManager, the burn succeeds against the caller's own balance — but the caller can also pass any `childToken` address, and the burn is executed against `msg.sender` regardless of intent. More critically, the function is intended to be the L2→L1 exit path and should only be callable by the fxManager; without that check, the burn can be triggered by anyone, and combined with the missing root-side validation, the accounting between chains is not enforced.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `withdraw(childToken, amount)` directly. 2) Tunnel burns the attacker's tokens. 3) Attacker (or a colluding root-side caller) can then call `FxERC20RootTunnel.syncWithdraw` to release root tokens without a corresponding legitimate deposit.
hypotheses.impact: Unbacked release of root-chain tokens; bridge insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `withdraw` to the trusted fxManager and require the burn to be part of a verified cross-chain message.

hypotheses.title: AgentFactoryV4.initialize callable by anyone to seize admin
hypotheses.description: `initialize` is `public initializer` with no access control. If the proxy is deployed and `initialize` is not called atomically (or is front-run), any external actor can call it, granting themselves `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` and setting `tokenImplementation`, `veTokenImplementation`, `daoImplementation`, `assetToken`, `nft`, `_vault`, `_tokenAdmin`, `_uniswapRouter`, and `_tokenSupplyParams`/`_tokenTaxParams`. This gives the attacker full control over all future agent deployments and the ability to point implementations at malicious contracts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes proxy deployment. 2) Front-runs the intended `initialize` with their own params. 3) Attacker becomes admin; sets `tokenImplementation` to a malicious contract that steals user funds on `initialize`/`addInitialLiquidity`. 4) All subsequent `proposeAgent`/`executeApplication` calls deploy attacker-controlled tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Complete protocol takeover: theft of user `assetToken` deposits, malicious agent tokens, drained vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deploy and initialize atomically, or add an `onlyOwner`/factory guard to `initialize` (e.g., require `_msgSender() == expectedDeployer`).

hypotheses.title: dcaSell computes minOutput from amountToSwap instead of expected asset output
hypotheses.description: `dcaSell` computes `minOutput = (amountToSwap * (DENOM - slippage)) / DENOM` where `amountToSwap` is denominated in `taxToken`, but `_swapForAsset` passes this value as `minOutput` for the `assetToken` side of a `taxToken -> assetToken` swap. The two tokens have unrelated decimals and prices, so `minOutput` is essentially meaningless — most of the time it either blocks every swap (`minOutput` too large) or provides zero protection when taxToken has fewer decimals / higher unit price than assetToken. Additionally, `dcaSell` performs `_swapForAsset(agentId, minOutput, maxOverride)` but `_swapForAsset` internally recomputes `amountToSwap` from storage and ignores any parameter binding between the computed value and the actual swap amount.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker sandwiches the executor's `dcaSell` transaction: front-run swap pushes the pool price down, the tax swap clears the (nonsensical) `minOutput` threshold, back-run restores the price. Because `minOutput` is derived from taxToken units, the protection is effectively absent in most configurations.
hypotheses.impact: Sale of accumulated tax tokens at manipulated prices, draining value from the agent creator and treasury.
hypotheses.recommendation: Derive `minOutput` from `router.getAmountsOut(amountToSwap, path)[1]` (or a trusted oracle), and apply the slippage factor to that expected output, not to the input amount.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV2._prepareAgentsRewards loops over all agents, DoS on distribution
hypotheses.description: `distributeRewards` calls `_prepareAgentsRewards`, which loops `for (uint256 virtualId = 1; virtualId <= totalAgents; virtualId++)` where `totalAgents = nft.totalSupply()`. As the number of minted agents grows, this loop will eventually exceed the block gas limit, making `distributeRewards` (and therefore all reward distribution) permanently uncallable. There is no pagination or batching.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user) mints many agents via `AgentFactoryV4.proposeAgent`/`executeApplication` (or via `initFromToken`), each requiring only the `applicationThreshold` of asset token. 2) Once `totalSupply()` is large enough (thousands), any call to `distributeRewards` reverts with out-of-gas. 3) All reward distribution halts; stakers/validators/contributors can never be paid.
hypotheses.impact: Reward distribution permanently frozen; protocol rewards and staker/validator rewards become unclaimable because no new rewards can be recorded.
hypotheses.recommendation: Replace the full loop with a paginated/batched distribution mechanism, or track eligible agents in an enumerable set that can be iterated in bounded chunks.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV3.getClaimableStakerRewards division by zero freezes claims
hypotheses.description: In `getClaimableStakerRewards`, the calculation `stakerReward = (agentReward.stakerAmount * stakedAmount) / agentReward.totalStaked` divides by `agentReward.totalStaked`, which is `nft.totalStaked(virtualId)` captured at distribution time. If `totalStaked == 0` at the time `_distributeAgentReward` is called (e.g., all stakers withdrew between the reward snapshot and distribution, or the agent was created with zero staked), the stored `totalStaked` is 0 and every subsequent call to `getClaimableStakerRewards` reverts with division by zero. Similarly `agentReward.totalProposals` can be 0 if the DAO has no proposals, causing `(stakerReward * uptime) / agentReward.totalProposals` to revert.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any staker) stakes a minimal amount to make the agent eligible, then withdraws all stake before `distributeRewards` is called for that agent. 2) `_distributeAgentReward` records `totalStaked = 0` (or `totalProposals = 0` if no proposals exist). 3) Any call to `getClaimableStakerRewards` or `claimStakerRewards` for that virtualId reverts with division by zero. 4) The claim counter `claim.rewardCount` can never advance, so all future rewards for that virtualId are also unclaimable.
hypotheses.impact: Staker rewards for the affected virtualId are permanently unclaimable; the reward index is stuck and all subsequent rewards for that agent are also frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip distribution (or store a sentinel) when `totalStaked == 0` or `totalProposals == 0`, and guard the division in the claim functions.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV2._distributeValidatorRewards loops over unbounded validator set
hypotheses.description: `_distributeValidatorRewards` iterates `for (uint256 i = 0; i < validatorCount; i++)` where `validatorCount = nft.validatorCount(virtualId)`. Validators are added via `AgentNftV2.addValidator` (called from `AgentVeToken.stake`), which is permissionless — any staker can add themselves as a validator. An attacker can add a huge number of validators to a single virtualId, making `_distributeAgentRewards` (and thus `distributeRewardsForAgents`) revert with out-of-gas.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes a tiny amount of the LP token for a target virtualId with many distinct addresses (or repeatedly with new delegatees), each call adding a new validator via `registry.addValidator`. 2) `validatorCount(virtualId)` grows unbounded. 3) Any call to `distributeRewardsForAgents` for that virtualId reverts with out-of-gas, blocking reward distribution for that agent.
hypotheses.impact: Reward distribution for the targeted agent is permanently frozen; stakers/validators/contributors of that agent cannot receive rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Cap the number of validators per virtualId, or paginate validator reward distribution.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV3 staker/validator rewards can be claimed twice via rewardCount reset
hypotheses.description: `getClaimableStakerRewards` uses `numRewards = Math.min(LOOP_LIMIT + claim.rewardCount, getAgentRewardCount(virtualId))`. If the number of agent rewards exceeds `LOOP_LIMIT`, only the first `LOOP_LIMIT` are processed and `claim.rewardCount` is set to `numRewards`. On the next call, `claim.rewardCount` is the new starting point, so the loop continues correctly. However, `claimStakerRewards` sets `claim.rewardCount = numRewards` unconditionally, and `getClaimableStakerRewards` returns `totalClaimable` computed only over the processed range. There is no issue with the loop itself, but the `_stakerClaims` mapping is keyed by `(account, virtualId)` and `claimAllStakerRewards` iterates `virtualIds` — if the same `virtualId` appears twice in the input array, the second iteration recomputes `getClaimableStakerRewards` from the already-updated `claim.rewardCount`, so no double claim. The real flaw: `getClaimableStakerRewards` divides by `agentReward.totalProposals`, which can be zero if the DAO has no proposals, causing a division-by-zero revert that permanently blocks claims for that virtualId.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A virtualId is created with a DAO that has zero proposals. 2) `_distributeAgentReward` records `totalProposals = 0`. 3) Any staker calling `claimStakerRewards` hits `(stakerReward * uptime) / agentReward.totalProposals` and reverts. 4) Rewards are permanently frozen for that virtualId.
hypotheses.impact: Staker rewards permanently locked; reward tokens stuck in contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard against `totalProposals == 0` by treating uptime as 0 or skipping the reward entry.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV2 staker rewards double-counted via validator claim path
hypotheses.description: `_distributeValidatorRewards` stores the full validator-group reward in `_validatorRewards[validator][rewardId]`, but `_getClaimableStakerRewardsAt` also pays stakers out of the same `_validatorRewards[delegatee][reward.id]` bucket (scaled by `stakerShares`). The validator claim path `_getClaimableValidatorRewardsAt` then pays the validator `validatorGroupRewards * (DENOMINATOR - stakerShares) / DENOMINATOR` from the same bucket, so the same underlying amount is paid twice (once to stakers, once to the validator) without any deduction of what stakers already took.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker becomes a validator for a virtualId (or is the founder/delegatee). 2) Stakers delegate to attacker. 3) Rewards are distributed; stakers claim their share via `_claimStakerRewards`. 4) Attacker calls `_claimValidatorRewards` and receives `validatorGroupRewards * (1 - stakerShares)` on top of what stakers already drained from the same bucket. 5) Repeat across rewards until the rewardToken balance is exhausted.
hypotheses.impact: Reward token insolvency — later claimants (other validators/stakers) cannot withdraw because the contract's rewardToken balance is drained; protocol accounting is permanently wrong.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deduct staker-paid amounts from `_validatorRewards[validator][rewardId]` when stakers claim, or track staker and validator buckets separately so the same reward is never paid twice.

hypotheses.title: Staker rewards double-counted via validator delegation in AgentRewardV2
hypotheses.description: In `_getClaimableStakerRewardsAt`, the staker's claimable amount is computed as `(validatorGroupRewards * tokens / votes) * stakerShares / DENOMINATOR`, where `validatorGroupRewards = _validatorRewards[delegatee][reward.id]`. But `_validatorRewards[delegatee][rewardId]` was already set in `_distributeValidatorRewards` to the validator's full share (participation-adjusted). The staker then multiplies this by their token share of the delegatee's votes, and the validator separately claims `validatorGroupRewards * (DENOMINATOR - stakerShares) / DENOMINATOR` in `_getClaimableValidatorRewardsAt`. Because the validator's full reward is used as the base for staker payouts, the sum of staker claims across all delegators can exceed the validator's actual reward, and the validator still claims their own portion — the same reward tokens are paid out twice.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes a small amount and delegates to a validator. 2) Attacker (or any staker) calls `claimAllRewards` for the virtualId. 3) `_getClaimableStakerRewardsAt` returns `validatorGroupRewards * tokens / votes * stakerShares / DENOMINATOR`. 4) The validator also calls `_claimValidatorRewards` and receives `validatorGroupRewards * (DENOMINATOR - stakerShares) / DENOMINATOR`. 5) Total paid = validatorGroupRewards * stakerShares + validatorGroupRewards * (1 - stakerShares) = validatorGroupRewards, but stakers collectively receive `validatorGroupRewards * stakerShares` while the validator receives the remainder — however the staker formula uses the full `validatorGroupRewards` as base, so if `stakerShares` is high and multiple stakers exist, the contract pays out more than was allocated.
hypotheses.impact: Reward token pool is drained faster than intended; later claimers get nothing; protocol becomes insolvent on reward payouts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute staker rewards from `validatorGroupRewards * stakerShares / DENOMINATOR` first, then divide by votes, so the validator and staker shares are disjoint.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV2 _distributeAgentRewards rounding leaves dust unclaimable
hypotheses.description: `amount = (mainReward.amount * reward.totalStaked) / mainReward.totalStaked` rounds down per agent. Summing across all agents, the total distributed is strictly less than `mainReward.amount` whenever there are multiple agents. The remainder is never assigned to `protocolRewards` or any sink, so it is permanently stranded in the contract with no accounting entry.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an attacker, but any user can observe that `sum(agent amounts) < mainReward.amount` and the difference accumulates in the contract balance while `protocolRewards`/`validatorPoolRewards` do not reflect it. Over many distributions this becomes a large unclaimable balance.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of reward tokens (stranded, unaccounted); protocol accounting drifts from real holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the remainder and add it to `protocolRewards`, or compute the last agent's amount as `mainReward.amount - distributedSoFar`.

hypotheses.title: AgentTax.handleAgentTaxes uses getAmountsOut spot price with minOutput supplied by executor
hypotheses.description: `handleAgentTaxes` accepts a caller-supplied `minOutput` (0 in practice from any executor call) and calls `router.getAmountsOut(amountToSwap, path)` purely to check `length > 1`, not to bound output. The subsequent `swapExactTokensForTokens(amountToSwap, minOutput, path, ...)` therefore executes at whatever the pool spot price is at that moment, with no TWAP, oracle, or per-swap slippage guard value enforced by the contract itself.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted party cannot call `handleAgentTaxes` directly (only `EXECUTOR_ROLE`), but the same untrusted actor can sandwich the executor's transaction: front-run to skew the taxToken/assetToken pool, let the tax swap execute at the bad price, then back-run to restore the price.
hypotheses.impact: Tax collections are sold for less than fair value; the loss is borne by the agent's creator and protocol treasury (both receive the swapped assetToken).
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute a minimum acceptable output inside the contract from an independent reference price (e.g., a TWAP), rather than trusting the caller-supplied `minOutput`; also enforce non-zero minOutput.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV2._distributeContributorRewards loops over unbounded services
hypotheses.description: `_distributeContributorRewards` calls `nft.getAllServices(virtualId)` which returns all service NFTs owned by the agent's TBA, then loops over them twice. Services are minted via `ServiceNft.mint` which is callable by the agent's DAO. A malicious or compromised DAO (or a DAO whose members are griefers) can mint an unbounded number of service NFTs, making `_distributeAgentRewards` revert with out-of-gas.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker gains control of an agent's DAO (or is a member who can pass proposals). 2) Attacker repeatedly calls `ServiceNft.mint` via DAO proposals to add thousands of service NFTs to the agent's TBA. 3) `getAllServices` returns a huge array; `_distributeContributorRewards` reverts with out-of-gas. 4) Reward distribution for that agent is permanently frozen.
hypotheses.impact: Reward distribution for the targeted agent is permanently frozen; all stakers/validators/contributors of that agent lose access to rewards.
hypotheses.recommendation: Paginate service iteration or cap the number of services per agent.

hypotheses.title: AgentTax.handleAgentTaxes accepts arbitrary txhashes without on-chain verification
hypotheses.description: `handleAgentTaxes` records `taxHistory[txhash] = TaxHistory(agentId, amounts[i])` and credits `agentAmounts.amountCollected` based solely on the executor-supplied `txhashes` and `amounts`. There is no on-chain verification that the txhash corresponds to an actual tax payment, no signature, no chain-id binding, and no check that the same txhash was not already used on another chain or in another deployment. The only protection is the `EXECUTOR_ROLE`, but the txhash is not bound to the chain or contract, so a txhash valid on one chain can be replayed on another deployment of the same contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Executor (or a compromised executor key) submits a txhash that was already processed on a different chain/deployment. 2) `taxHistory[txhash].agentId` is 0 on this chain, so the check passes. 3) `agentAmounts.amountCollected` is inflated, and `_swapForAsset` swaps tax tokens that were not actually collected for this agent, draining the contract's tax token balance.
hypotheses.impact: Inflated tax accounting and potential draining of tax tokens held by the contract; cross-chain replay of tax credits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the txhash to `block.chainid` and `address(this)` (e.g., `keccak256(abi.encode(chainId, address(this), txhash))`) and verify the tax payment on-chain or via a signed message from the tax source.

hypotheses.title: LPRefund.refund accepts arbitrary txhashes without chain/contract binding
hypotheses.description: `refund` records `refunds[txhash] = amount` and transfers `taxToken` to `recipient` based only on executor-supplied `txhashes` and `amounts`. The txhash is not bound to `block.chainid` or `address(this)`, so the same txhash can be replayed across chains or across multiple deployments of `LPRefund`. There is no signature or on-chain verification that the txhash corresponds to an actual tax payment.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Executor submits a txhash already used on another chain/deployment. 2) `refunds[txhash]` is 0 on this chain, so the check passes. 3) `taxToken` is transferred to the recipient, draining the contract's balance.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-chain replay of refunds, draining the contract's tax token balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the txhash to `block.chainid` and `address(this)` before storing/checking it.

hypotheses.title: Genesis onGenesisSuccess allows repeated refunds via mapAddrToVirtuals underflow
hypotheses.description: `onGenesisSuccess` can be called multiple times (only `whenNotCancelled whenNotFailed whenEnded`), and on each call it iterates `refundVirtualsTokenUserAddresses` and does `mapAddrToVirtuals[user] -= refundVirtualsTokenUserAmounts[i]`. The check `mapAddrToVirtuals[user] >= refundVirtualsTokenUserAmounts[i]` prevents underflow, but the function does not track that a user has already been refunded. If the factory (trusted) passes the same user twice with amounts that sum to less than their committed balance, the user is refunded multiple times. More critically, `claimableAgentTokens[user]` is overwritten (not accumulated) on each call, so a user's previously-claimed agent tokens can be reset and re-claimed if `agentTokenAddress` is already set and the contract still holds tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Factory calls `onGenesisSuccess` with user A and refund amount X. 2) User A's `mapAddrToVirtuals` is reduced by X and they receive X virtual tokens. 3) Factory calls `onGenesisSuccess` again with user A and refund amount Y (Y <= remaining balance). 4) User A receives Y more virtual tokens. 5) Additionally, `claimableAgentTokens[A]` is overwritten each time, so if A already claimed, the new value can be claimed again.
hypotheses.impact: Virtual tokens drained from Genesis contract; agent tokens double-claimed; protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track per-user refunded amounts and accumulate `claimableAgentTokens` instead of overwriting; add a one-time finalization flag.

hypotheses.title: AgentToken tax pending counter drifts from actual contract balance
hypotheses.description: `projectTaxPendingSwap` is decremented proportionally in `_swapTax` on success, but `_taxProcessing` increments it by `uint128(projectTax)` — a downcast that silently truncates if `projectTax > type(uint128).max`. More importantly, `distributeTaxTokens` transfers `projectTaxPendingSwap` tokens out via `_transfer(..., false)` but does not decrement `_balances[address(this)]` for the tax portion separately — it relies on `_transfer` doing so. However, `_swapTax`'s proportional reduction uses `projectTaxPendingSwap * swapBalance / contractBalance`, where `contractBalance` includes tokens that are NOT tax (e.g., tokens sent directly to the contract). This causes `projectTaxPendingSwap` to be reduced by less than the actual tax tokens swapped, leaving a phantom pending balance that can later be claimed via `distributeTaxTokens`, draining non-tax tokens held by the contract.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker sends a small amount of AgentToken directly to the contract address (donation). 2) `contractBalance` now exceeds `projectTaxPendingSwap`. 3) On next autoswap, `projectTaxPendingSwap -= projectTaxPendingSwap * swapBalance / contractBalance` reduces pending by less than the tax actually swapped. 4) Attacker calls `distributeTaxTokens()` repeatedly; each call transfers `projectTaxPendingSwap` tokens to `projectTaxRecipient`, eventually draining the donated tokens and any other tokens held by the contract.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of tokens held by the contract (donations, or tokens meant for other purposes); accounting drift between `projectTaxPendingSwap` and real tax holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track tax tokens in a separate accounting variable and only reduce `projectTaxPendingSwap` by the exact tax amount swapped, not a proportional share of total balance.

hypotheses.title: Genesis.onGenesisSuccess double-counts refunds against reserve on repeat calls
hypotheses.description: `onGenesisSuccess` can be called multiple times (only guarded by `refundUserCountForFailed == 0` and `whenEnded`). On the first call, `isFirstLaunch` is true and `requiredVirtualsBalance = totalRefundAmount + reserveAmount`. On subsequent calls, `isFirstLaunch` is false and `requiredVirtualsBalance = totalRefundAmount`. However, `mapAddrToVirtuals[user]` is decremented by the refund amount each call, so a second call with the same refund arrays will fail the `mapAddrToVirtuals >= refundAmount` check — UNLESS the caller passes different (smaller) refund amounts for users who still have balance. More critically, `claimableAgentTokens[user]` is *overwritten* (not accumulated) on each call, so a second call with a distribution array can reset a user's claimable amount to a smaller value, and the previously-allocated tokens remain in the contract but are no longer claimable by anyone — they can be swept by `withdrawLeftAssetsAfterFinalized`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly attacker-controlled (only FACTORY_ROLE), but the accounting flaw means: 1) First call distributes agent tokens to users via `claimableAgentTokens`. 2) Second call with a different distribution array overwrites `claimableAgentTokens` for some users to 0 or smaller values. 3) The orphaned agent tokens remain in the contract and are withdrawable by admin via `withdrawLeftAssetsAfterFinalized`. Users lose their allocated tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Users' allocated agent tokens are silently overwritten and become withdrawable by admin; loss of user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `onGenesisSuccess` idempotent (revert if `agentTokenAddress != 0` and distribution already done), or accumulate `claimableAgentTokens` instead of overwriting.

hypotheses.title: AgentToken token-approval to router set before liquidity, price set by contract's own balance
hypotheses.description: `_addInitialLiquidity` uses `addLiquidity(..., 0, 0, ...)` and immediately sets `_autoSwapInProgress = false`. Once funded, the initial price of the AgentToken in the pairToken pool is whatever ratio the contract holds. There is no minimum-liquidity or price sanity check, and the fundedDate check only blocks transfers to the pair before this call — after both the LP and other pools (`addLiquidityPool`) are present, nothing anchors the pool price to any external reference.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker (including the LP recipient via a registered additional pool) can call `addLiquidityPool` only via owner/factory, so not directly. However, once any additional pool is added, an attacker can trade on whichever pool has the thinnest reserves and arbitrage the difference against the primary pair; because the token tax module reads `isLiquidityPool`, a maliciously-added thin pool effectively lets the attacker feed `_autoSwap` with manipulated prices (see also finding 1).
hypotheses.impact: Post-listing arbitrage/price manipulation of the token relative to `pairToken`, allowing extraction of value from LPs and from tax swaps.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum liquidity amount and a sanity band on the observed initial price (or, at minimum, use non-zero amountMin/amountB in `addLiquidity`) and gate `addLiquidityPool` behind a timelock to prevent thin-pool attacks.

hypotheses.title: FRouter.getAmountsOut can return inflated output due to constant-k recomputation
hypotheses.description: `getAmountsOut` reads `pair.getReserves()` and `pair.kLast()` and computes output as `reserveA - k / (reserveB + amountIn)` (or the mirror). Because `FPair.k` is never updated on swaps (see `FPair.swap`, which preserves `_pool.k`), the effective pricing uses a stale `k` that assumes reserves always move on the constant-product curve. In practice `k` is set once at `mint` and never refreshed, so after any swap the pool's real invariant drifts; the returned quote is therefore inconsistent with the true reserves and can be arbitrarily wrong relative to the actual amounts the pair will transfer.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted trader uses `getAmountsOut` (or front-runs a caller who relies on it) to obtain a favorable quote: the stale `k` can make the formula output larger than the true constant-product output, and an attacker can execute `router.buy`/`router.sell` (via the bonding flow that routes through the router) to extract the difference. Since `FPair.transferAsset`/`transferTo` blindly send whatever the router asks, the pool will pay out more than the reserve implies.
hypotheses.impact: Drain of pool reserves (`tokenA`/`tokenB`) because swaps can clear more output than constant-product math permits; loss is borne by other LPs and the bonding curve participants.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `_pool.k` after every swap in `FPair.swap`, or in `FRouter.getAmountsOut` use live reserves and the standard `x*y=k` formula rather than a stale `kLast()`.

hypotheses.title: AeroAdaptor ignores `path` and always routes tokenIn->tokenOut, mispricing arbitrary callers
hypotheses.description: `AeroAdaptor.swapExactTokensForTokens` and `getAmountsOut` ignore the caller-supplied `path` array entirely and always construct a single-hop route `tokenIn -> tokenOut` from the adaptor's immutable state. Any caller (e.g., `AgentTax`/`BondingTax`, whose `router` may point at this adaptor) that expects the router semantics of UniswapV2 (multi-hop, arbitrary pairs) will silently get a different swap than requested. In particular, if the caller requests a 2-hop path but the adaptor's tokenIn/tokenOut pair has no pool or is arbitrarily priced, the `amountOutMin` check inside the caller is bypassed in a different direction.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted actor trades the adaptor's fixed pair in the Aerodrome pool to move its price; when `AgentTax`/`BondingTax` uses the adaptor as its router, the tax swap is executed at the manipulated fixed-pair price rather than the intended path, and the caller's `minOutput` (derived from `getAmountsOut`, which also ignores the path) will be stale or zero.
hypotheses.impact: Tax and fee swaps misprice consistently; funds can be sold for less than expected on every transaction routed through the adaptor.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that `path[0] == tokenIn` and `path[path.length-1] == tokenOut`, and use the actual `path` to build routes; revert on unsupported paths instead of silently substituting.

hypotheses.title: AgentInference.promptMulti reuses stale agentTba when agentId repeats non-consecutively
hypotheses.description: `promptMulti` caches `agentTba` and only refreshes it when `prevAgentId != agentId`. However, `prevAgentId` is never updated inside the loop, so it remains 0 for the entire loop. This means the cache is refreshed on every iteration (since `0 != agentId` for any non-zero agentId), which is functionally correct but the intended optimization is broken. More importantly, if `agentId` is 0, `agentNft.virtualInfo(0).tba` is used, and the transfer goes to the zero-agent TBA. The function does not validate that `agentId` is a valid, existing virtual ID, so funds can be sent to a non-existent agent's TBA.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `promptMulti` with `agentIds[i] = 0` (or any non-existent ID). 2) `agentNft.virtualInfo(0).tba` returns `address(0)` or a stale TBA. 3) `token.safeTransferFrom(sender, agentTba, amounts[i])` sends tokens to the zero address or an unintended recipient, and `inferenceCount[0]` is incremented.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds to an unintended/zero address; incorrect inference accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that each `agentId` is a valid virtual ID (e.g., `agentId > 0 && agentId < agentNft.nextVirtualId()`) and update `prevAgentId = agentId` inside the loop.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV2 distributeRewardsForAgents can be called repeatedly for same reward
hypotheses.description: `_distributeAgentRewards` has a guard `if (reward.validatorAmount > 0 || reward.contributorAmount > 0) return;` to prevent double distribution. However, if `amount` for a virtualId is 0 (e.g., `mainReward.amount * reward.totalStaked / mainReward.totalStaked` rounds to 0), then `reward.validatorAmount` and `reward.contributorAmount` remain 0, and the guard does not trigger. A subsequent call to `distributeRewardsForAgents` for the same `mainRewardIndex` and `virtualId` will re-enter `_distributeAgentRewards`, recompute the same 0 amounts, and call `_distributeValidatorRewards` and `_distributeContributorRewards` again. While the amounts are 0, `_distributeContributorRewards` still pushes service impacts and updates `_serviceRewards`, and `_distributeValidatorRewards` still adds to `validatorPoolRewards` (0 in this case). More importantly, if `reward.totalStaked` is 0 (agent below threshold but still in `_rewards`), division by zero reverts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A virtualId has `totalStaked` below `stakeThreshold` at distribution time, so it is skipped in `_prepareAgentsRewards` and no reward entry is created. 2) Alternatively, a virtualId with `totalStaked > 0` but `mainReward.amount * totalStaked / grandTotalStaked == 0` (very small amount) leaves `validatorAmount == 0`. 3) Anyone (gov) calls `distributeRewardsForAgents` again; the guard fails to block, and `_distributeContributorRewards` re-runs, double-counting service impacts.
hypotheses.impact: Service reward impacts double-counted; reward distribution skewed; potential division-by-zero revert.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an explicit `distributed` boolean flag per Reward entry, or check `reward.id != 0` before processing.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV2 _distributeAgentRewards can be re-run for same mainRewardIndex
hypotheses.description: The double-entry guard only checks `reward.validatorAmount > 0 || reward.contributorAmount > 0`. If `settings.contributorShares == 0` and `settings.stakerShares == 0` (or the computed `amount` is 0), `validatorAmount` and `contributorAmount` remain 0, so the guard never trips. `distributeRewardsForAgents` is `onlyGov`, but the same virtualId can be passed multiple times in the array, and the guard also fails to prevent re-entry when amounts round to zero.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Gov calls `distributeRewardsForAgents(mainRewardIndex, [v, v, v, ...])` with the same virtualId repeated. 2) Because `reward.validatorAmount`/`contributorAmount` are still 0 after the first pass (zero-share settings or zero amount), the guard does not block subsequent iterations. 3) `_distributeValidatorRewards` and `_distributeContributorRewards` run repeatedly, inflating `_validatorRewards` and `_serviceRewards` for the same reward.
hypotheses.impact: Reward accounting is inflated; validators/contributors can claim more than the distributed amount, draining the rewardToken balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track a per-reward `distributed` boolean (or compare `reward.mainIndex` against a stored processed flag) instead of relying on non-zero amounts.

hypotheses.title: AgentTax handleAgentTaxes swaps full balance ignoring per-agent accounting
hypotheses.description: `_swapForAsset` computes `amountToSwap = agentAmounts.amountCollected - agentAmounts.amountSwapped` but then checks `balance >= amountToSwap` against the contract-wide `taxToken` balance, and swaps `amountToSwap` from the shared pool. If multiple agents' taxes are held in the same contract, one agent's swap can consume another agent's tax tokens, and `agentAmounts.amountSwapped` is only incremented for the calling agent. The contract-wide balance check does not enforce per-agent isolation.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Two agents A and B accumulate tax tokens in the same AgentTax contract. 2) Executor calls `handleAgentTaxes` for agent A with a large `amountToSwap`. 3) The swap consumes tokens that were collected for agent B. 4) Agent B's `amountCollected - amountSwapped` remains positive but the tokens are gone; B's swap later reverts with "Insufficient balance".
hypotheses.impact: Cross-agent fund commingling; one agent's taxes are used to pay another's swap, and the second agent's taxes become unswappable (frozen).
hypotheses.recommendation: Track per-agent taxToken balances separately, or transfer each agent's tax tokens to a per-agent escrow before swapping.

hypotheses.title: Genesis onGenesisSuccess can be re-entered to double-distribute agent tokens
hypotheses.description: `onGenesisSuccess` is `nonReentrant` and `onlyRole(FACTORY_ROLE)`, but the `isFirstLaunch` check is `agentTokenAddress == address(0)`. On the first call, `agentTokenAddress` is set only after `executeBondingCurveApplication` returns. If the factory (or a compromised factory role) calls `onGenesisSuccess` twice in the same transaction via a callback, the second call sees `agentTokenAddress != 0` and skips launch, but still re-runs the refund and distribution loops. More critically, `claimableAgentTokens[user] = amount` overwrites rather than accumulates, and `mapAddrToVirtuals[user] -= amount` can underflow if the same user appears twice in the refund array.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Factory calls `onGenesisSuccess` with the same user address repeated in `refundVirtualsTokenUserAddresses`. 2) First iteration subtracts `amount` from `mapAddrToVirtuals[user]`; second iteration subtracts again. 3) If the user's committed amount is less than the sum, the subtraction underflows (Solidity 0.8 reverts) — but if the user committed enough, the user receives double the refund while `mapAddrToVirtuals` is decremented twice.
hypotheses.impact: Users can receive more virtual tokens than they committed; the contract's virtualToken balance is drained, leaving other participants unable to claim refunds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Deduplicate addresses or accumulate refunds per address before transferring; use a per-address `refunded` flag.

hypotheses.title: AgentToken _autoSwap can be triggered by attacker to drain tax tokens
hypotheses.description: `_autoSwap` is called on every transfer and triggers a swap of accumulated tax tokens to `pairToken` when `contractBalance >= swapThresholdInTokens`. The swap sends output to `projectTaxRecipient` and reduces `projectTaxPendingSwap` proportionally. An attacker can repeatedly transfer small amounts to push `contractBalance` above the threshold, forcing swaps at unfavorable prices (especially if the attacker sandwiches the swap). Since `_eligibleForSwap` excludes transfers from/to the router and liquidity pools, the attacker can use a normal EOA transfer to trigger the swap. The attacker can also manipulate the AMM price before the swap to extract value from the tax tokens.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker accumulates tax tokens in the contract by making buys/sells. 2) Attacker sandwiches a transfer that triggers `_autoSwap` with a large buy/sell on the AMM to move the price. 3) The swap executes at the manipulated price, and the attacker profits from the price impact. 4) `projectTaxPendingSwap` is reduced, but the actual value received by `projectTaxRecipient` is less than fair.
hypotheses.impact: Tax tokens swapped at manipulated prices; project tax recipient receives less value; MEV extraction.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a private mempool or commit-reveal for auto-swaps, or add a minimum output check based on an oracle.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV3 claim functions transfer 0 and can be griefed via LOOP_LIMIT
hypotheses.description: `numRewards = Math.min(LOOP_LIMIT + claim.rewardCount, getAgentRewardCount(virtualId))`. When `claim.rewardCount` is already at or above `getAgentRewardCount`, `numRewards` equals the current count and the loop body never executes, returning 0. But `claimStakerRewards` still writes `claim.rewardCount = numRewards` and calls `safeTransfer(account, 0)`. More importantly, if a user has more than `LOOP_LIMIT` unclaimed rewards, they can only advance `rewardCount` by `LOOP_LIMIT` per call, and each call re-reads `getAgentRewardCount` — but the loop bound uses `LOOP_LIMIT + claim.rewardCount`, which is correct only if `claim.rewardCount` is the last processed index. If a reward is added between calls, the user may skip rewards.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or any user) triggers many reward distributions so `getAgentRewardCount(v)` grows. 2) A staker calls `claimStakerRewards`; only `LOOP_LIMIT` rewards are processed. 3) If new rewards are pushed between calls, the index arithmetic `LOOP_LIMIT + claim.rewardCount` can skip rewards that were added in between, permanently losing them for that staker.
hypotheses.impact: Stakers permanently lose claimable rewards; rewardToken remains stuck in the contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Iterate from `claim.rewardCount` to `min(claim.rewardCount + LOOP_LIMIT, count)` and always set `claim.rewardCount` to the actual last processed index.

hypotheses.title: AgentRewardV3 staker+validator rewards exceed deposited amount due to independent rounding
hypotheses.description: `_distributeAgentReward` splits `amount` into `stakerAmount = amount * stakerShares / DENOMINATOR` and `validatorAmount = amount - stakerAmount`. However, `getClaimableStakerRewards` computes `stakerReward = (agentReward.stakerAmount * stakedAmount) / totalStaked` then multiplies by `uptime / totalProposals`, and `getClaimableValidatorRewards` computes `validatorReward = (agentReward.validatorAmount * votes) / totalStaked` then `* uptime / totalProposals`. Because `stakedAmount` and `votes` are independent per-account values and `uptime` is per-account, the sum of all staker claims can exceed `stakerAmount` when `totalStaked` used at distribution time differs from the sum of `stakedAmount` at claim time (e.g., stakers withdraw between distribution and claim). The `totalStaked` snapshot is taken at distribution, but `getPastBalanceOf` at `reward.blockNumber` may not sum to it if balances changed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker stakes, waits for a reward distribution. 2) Attacker (or colluding accounts) withdraws most stake after distribution but before claim. 3) At claim, `getPastBalanceOf(account, reward.blockNumber)` still returns the historical balance, so claims are correct per-account — but if any staker's historical balance is missing (e.g., staked after distribution), the denominator `totalStaked` over-counts, under-paying; conversely if `totalStaked` under-counts (stakers withdrew before distribution snapshot), claims over-pay. The mismatch between `agentReward.totalStaked` and the sum of `getPastBalanceOf` at `reward.blockNumber` causes systematic over/under payment.
hypotheses.impact: Reward pool can be drained beyond deposited amount (insolvency) or stakers under-paid.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the same snapshot source for `totalStaked` and per-account balances, and cap total claims at `stakerAmount`/`validatorAmount`.

hypotheses.title: Bonding._openTradingOnUniswap reads pair reserves after graduation, enables stale reserve usage in same-block
hypotheses.description: In `buy`, after the router swap updates the pair reserves, `_openTradingOnUniswap` is invoked (when `newReserveA <= gradThreshold`). Inside, it calls `router.graduate(tokenAddress)` which transfers the pair's asset tokens to `Bonding`, then transfers them to `agentFactory` and creates the agent token. The graduation reads `pair.assetBalance()` and `pair.balance()` from `FPair`, but `FRouter.graduate` calls `FPair.transferAsset(msg.sender, assetBalance)` WITHOUT updating `_pool.reserve1`, so the FPair's internal reserves no longer match actual token balances. Any subsequent `getAmountsOut`/`buy`/`sell` on this pair reads stale reserves. Since `tokenInfo[tokenAddress].trading` is set to false and `tradingOnUniswap` true, further `buy`/`sell` are blocked — but `unwrapToken` still reads `factory.getPair` and processes balances. The attacker path: a same-block buy that pushes reserveA to graduation threshold causes graduation with drained asset tokens, but the attacker has already received the tokens via `transferTo`. The real issue: after graduation, the FERC20 in pair is burned and agents issued, leaving FPair state inconsistent.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker buys enough to trigger graduation; then in same block any trader using stale `getReserves()` gets manipulated pricing, but trading is disabled post-graduation so no direct trade. The post-graduation state inconsistency is exploitable if any contract queries `getReserves()` for pricing — none in-scope does.
hypotheses.impact: Stale reserves; potential incorrect pricing if reused.
hypotheses.recommendation: Zero out the pair reserves in `graduate`.
